criteria.title: Indicates author name(s)
criteria.description: The name of the applicant, the author(s) of the DMP, is/are clearly indicated. This need not coincide with the person responsible for the DMP (stated later, see G.resp.5 and G.resp.6). If DMP responsibility is given to an individual, this point is still not fulfilled is there is no explicit statement that that person has also written the DMP.
criteria.rationale: Without author names, it is impossible to know who created the DMP, or contact them.

criteria.title: Indicates Author(s) contact information
criteria.description: At least one author has their full contact information clearly stated. This could also be the contact information of their institutions. Defining an ORCiD record for the author automatically fulfills this criterion, as the ORCiD record is usually kept updated with the current email addresses and other contact information of the author. Similar to A.sid.1, if a person is designated to be responsible for the DMP, the point is not fulfilled if they are not also explicitly stated that they have authored the DMP.
criteria.rationale: Without author contact information, it is impossible to contact them in case comments or concerns regarding the DMP arise.

Score 0 if the PID service is obscure or has the possibility to not be permanent or promptly updated (e.g. W3C PURLs). In Similar to A.sid.1, if a person is designated to be responsible for the DMP, the point is not fulfilled if they are not also explicitly stated that they have authored the DMP.
criteria.rationale: OrcIDs and other PIDs pinpoint with exact precision the author(s) of the document.

criteria.title: IA - Indicates the funding program and funding body
criteria.scoring: Applies only when the DMP is written for a funded project with a specific program (e.g. Horizon Europe). Scored as 1 (fulfilled), 0 (not fulfilled) or NA (not applicable).
criteria.description: Clearly states the funding program type. Clearly states the organization(s) that are funding the project. Contact information for the funding agencies is not required if they are internationally recognizable (e.g. Horizon Europe from the European Research Council). Logos and other non-explicit indications could satisfy this criterium if they are sufficiently obvious and include the funding body name.
criteria.rationale: Funding body may have an effect on data handling and sharing.

criteria.rationale: DMPs may change over time. It is important to keep track of the changes appointed to them.

criteria.description: Includes the project identifier (in the funding program context) or another PID related to the project. This can also be arbitrary and local (e.g. at institution level). This PID must be sufficient to keep track of the DMP throughout its various versions.
criteria.rationale: PIDs are essential in keeping track of various aspects of the project, and it is important that the DMP contains this information for cross-referencing purposes.

criteria.title: Lists all types of gathered data
criteria.description: Fulfilled if all data kinds used by the project are listed. A data “kind” is the nature of the data being collected, the phenomenon or trace that is trying to be captured. It is hard to determine if all kinds of data are actually listed when the DMP is first created. If possible, check the actual results or with the authors to see if the list is accurate or not.
criteria.rationale: The DMP is used to plan the management of each different data type. A list of these types is essential in order to do so.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples

criteria.title: Lists all formats of gathered data
criteria.description: Similar to B.dtyp.1, but regarding digital data formats (e.g. .pdf, .png) or, alternatively, on the types of physical objects stored, catalogued based on type and other storage features or requirements. One preferred data format should be specified. Other formats for the same type of data can be indicated, if properly explained.
criteria.rationale: The data formats are essential in determining how well they might be handled internally or shared externally.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: The project will use three main data formats: .csv for tables, .wav for audio recordings and .png for images.
For data tables, they will be stored as .csv. When the format of the data is too large to be stored as .csv, .parquet data files will be used.

Data will be stored in the most efficient format available (*too generic*).

criteria.title: Lists all combinations of data type and format separately
criteria.description: This point specifically refers to listing all data kinds and data format combinations, along with their descriptions. This is usually done as a table, but the format is not important.
criteria.rationale: Each data type may be collected with different data formats. Explicitly handling different data format-and-type combination separately is important to determine the impact of these decisions precisely.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: The project will handle the following types of data: brain scans of patients during rest or exertion in voxel format (.vxl), brain scans of rats during rest or exertion in voxel format (.vxl), metadata regarding samples in tabular formats (.xlsx, .xls) and a data vocabulary as a BLOB dictionary (.dblob).

criteria.title: Uses only open or widely used community formats
criteria.description:
Only open formats or widely used, common community formats are specified. A list of suggested formats for various common data types can be seen in Appendix 1 of this document. More specific formats for specialized topics must be evaluated singularly, such as by using FAIRSharing.org (https://fairsharing.org/) or similar services. The score given to this criterium cannot be higher than that given for B.dtyp.2. A novel data format can be considered “open” if the project also plans on sharing it as a result, but the creation of new formats must be appropriately explained as impossible to avoid.
This criterium is fulfilled also if closed data types are used *during* the project, but are explicitly changed for preservation and sharing purposes (e.g. usage of Word documents that are then exported into PDF/A-1a for preservation). A short explanation of the procedure may also be included.
This criterium also applies to data packaging formats, like compression algorithms.
criteria.rationale: Open and community formats are a necessary prerogative for effective long-term preservation and interoperability.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: The project will handle the following types of data: brain scans of patients during rest or exertion in voxel format (.vxl), brain scans of rats during rest or exertion in voxel format (.vxl), metadata regarding samples in tabular formats (.csv) and a data vocabulary as a JSON dictionary (.json).

The project will handle written documents. They will be created as Word (.docx) documents during the project but will be shared with the Open Document Format (.odf). Conversion issues will be handled appropriately.

(*usage of some obscure or proprietary data types, .xslx, .dblob)*

criteria.rationale: The choice of data format must be pondered sufficiently before that particular data format can be used.

criteria.rationale: Not all encodings or subtypes are suitable for sharing.

criteria.title: Addresses how data will be searched for reuse
criteria.description:
Fulfilled if at least one of the following is true:
In all cases, it is up to the reviewer to decide if the description is sufficiently exhaustive or not. Full scores are given to true efforts to avoid the generation of data, or sufficiently clear explanations of why generating data is not avoidable. Partial points are given if some types of data are covered, while some other points are not.
criteria.rationale: Re-using data is fundamental to avoid wasteful data re-generation. Additionally, a proper search strategy (i.e. setting the *desiderata* for the nature of data) informs data collection efforts and metadata choices.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Five major databases for transcriptomic data will be searched for RNA-seq data from HMEC-1 cell lines. Only data with at least 1M reads per sample will be suitable... (*and more details, especially regarding sampling)*

Five major databases have been previously searched for reusable data. In particular ... (*details of data selection and quality criteria).* Of the 8 datasets that matched our search parameters, none fulfilled our data quality criteria.
This project aims to expand our current body of knowledge regarding data on the tensile strengths of various materials. Generating new data is one of the main objectives of the project.
This is a pioneering project aiming to sample ice crystal formations on the north pole of Mars. No similar projects have ever been performed.

examples.title: Partially Fulfilled examples
examples: We searched five major databases for RNA-seq data regarding HMEC-1 cell lines and found no suitable data for reuse (*too little detail*).
We will use 2 types of data, Y and Y’. We searched X database for Y data with Z selection criteria (*only one data type was covered*).

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: We will search thematic databases for reusable data (*not enough information on selection criteria*)*.*
We expect no data to be reusable for this project (*no effort is documented to find reusable data*).
*No information is given on searching for existing data to reuse.*

criteria.title: Explains reusable data selection criteria
criteria.description: Clearly explains the criteria in place that data must have to be reused. Alternatively, clearly details the discard criteria that would make data unsuitable for reuse.
criteria.rationale: Properly determined discard criteria (i.e. setting the *desiderata* for the nature of data) informs data collection efforts and metadata choices.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data regarding HMEC-1 cell lines from a number of selected providers will be considered for reuse. The maximum passage number allowed will be 5. FASTQ files with at least 1M reads will be considered.

examples.title: Partially Fulfilled examples
examples: *Details are not given for all data types.*
Data regarding HMEC-1 cells lines will be selected if it fulfills certain quality parameters (*Too generic*).

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No reference to specific quality criteria for selection*.

criteria.title: Explains why new data needs to be gathered
criteria.description:
Clearly explains why new data must be gathered for the project. Provides evidence that previous searches for reusable data have failed and/or that specific requirements of the project require novel data to be recorded. Argues for the creation of each data type explicitly, or, alternatively, addresses novel data collection as a whole and (briefly) addresses its use during the project.
Project always generate new data (even just analysis code is new data), so at least one novel data type will always be there.
criteria.rationale: New data should be minimized. Storage, FAIRification and handling of data comes at a cost, and this cost should be reduced. This point allows the author to consciously decide if all data types are required for the project’s goals.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: This project aims to monitor Macaque mating calls in modern day Gibraltar. New data must be collected.
No suitable data regarding the genetic makeup of B. leonensis is available, making new data collection impossible to avoid.

While bibliographies of the works of Alighieri are common, significant doubts have arisen in recent years that a significant portion of his works are omitted *(including citation),* making the curation of a new bibliography required.
This project uses previously published data and performs a metanalysis on it. This process in inherently novel and so is the result.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No explanation on the requirement for new data to be collected.*
*One or more data types are not sufficiently explained.*

criteria.title: Explains how data provenance will be tracked
criteria.scoring: Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description:
Clearly considers how data provenance (i.e. person that collected the data, location, time, date, processing steps, measurement device, etc...) will be recorded, often at the moment of recording.
What specific information is “provenance” changes between fields, so it’s up to the reviewer to decide if enough provenance is planned to allow effective reuse.
criteria.rationale: When new data is created, its provenance is one of the most important metadata features.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: The location, time and the characteristics of the camera apparatus used to generate the pictures are automatically saved. Authorship information will be recorded separately when images are stored in the central server.
Specific data provenance collection forms will be developed for MRI scans, will be filled as MRI scans are performed and will be saved together with the resulting data.
Code development will happen on GitHub, which automatically tracks the time and authorship of each commit.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples

criteria.title: Indicates if required software will be preserved
criteria.description:
Explicitly indicates if particular software is required to read, understand or reuse the data. If so, clearly indicates the version(s) required, the location of the source code and other information to identify the software. If containerization or other software packaging solutions are used, this information may be omitted (see B.compat.2).
Common data formats expected to be readable (or easily converted) into the far future are exempt from this requirement, although a simple statement considering this problem (and dismissing it) is still required.
If proprietary software which cannot be shared must be used, a strong, detailed argument for why its use is unavoidable must be provided.
If multiple data types are involved, even one without its required software makes this criterium not fulfilled.
criteria.rationale: Some specialized data types require uncommon software to be shared alongside it, or the data is inaccessible.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: This project does not use any data formats that require uncommon software to be read or understood.
The software “readVoxels” is required to visualize and process the MRI voxel data.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples

*One or more required software are not detailed.*

criteria.title: IP - Indicates how required software will be preserved
criteria.scoring: Applicable only if specific software is required to access the data for preservation purposes (B.compat.1). If it is unknown whether software is required or not, score this as 0. Scored as 1 (fulfilled) or 0 (not fulfilled).
criteria.description: If specific software is required to be preserved alongside the data, the DMP specifies how this will be achieved. Judgement on the e0ffectiveness of the identified solution is left to reviewer expertise. Consider if sufficient effort is shown to properly preserve the software and allow its use in the far future (e.g. using services such as Software Heritage).
criteria.rationale: If software is required, it must be preserved. Detailing how at the level of the DMP increases the likelihood that the issue will be addressed properly during the project.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: The software “readVoxels”, required to visualize and process the MRI voxel data will be containerized and shipped alongside the data proper.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No explanation on the need to store software is given.*
*One or more required software are not detailed.*
Software to access the data will be provided upon request (*too generic*).

criteria.title: Gives details of data volumes (bytes or numbers)
criteria.scoring: Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: Explicitly details the volume of the generated data, even in broad strokes.
criteria.rationale: Data volume informs a lot of storage and preservation choices. It may also warrant discussing specific storage solutions during active data management if big data is being processed.

criteria.title: Indicates which metadata will be provided
criteria.scoring: Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description:
Explicitly lists which metadata will be provided for the data. This criterium is purposefully generic as to allow less mature DMPs to be scored for a preliminary work regarding metadata. Also fulfilled by stating that ontologies and vocabularies will be searched for to best fit the (meta)data that is being collected, especially if the way this search will be performed is illustrated.
This is a “soft” version of C.meta.2.
criteria.rationale: A list of required metadata for all data types is required, but it is sometimes hard to provide them in high detail while the DMP is being redacted.

criteria.title: Indicates metadata standards for each data kind or type
criteria.scoring: Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description:
Explicitly lists all metadata for each (expressed) data type/format combination or, if these are not given, for each data type. Multiple data type/format combinations may use the same metadata schema. Also fulfilled if metadata schemas or existing ontologies are used. The relevance and sufficient specificity of the proposed metadata is left to reviewer expertise.
This is the “hard” version of C.meta.1.
criteria.rationale: It is important to decide which metadata to record for each data type before data is acquired. Some kinds of data cannot be saved after data is collected(or get increasingly harder to be recorded).

criteria.title: Defines file naming conventions
criteria.description:
Clearly specifies file naming conventions used for each data type or throughout the project. If the data is stored in different locations (see D.stor.1), specifies where the naming conventions will apply.
Reason: Especially in multi-partner projects, file naming conventions keep all homogeneous files recognizable and make knowing the structure and format of each file easier.

examples: Throughout the HOR project, files will follow the following naming convention:... (*Includes a pattern description for each naming convention*)

criteria.title: Addresses standard folder structures

criteria.rationale: Standardized folder structure significantly limits the possibility of losing data due to poor organization, especially if it is documented. It also makes every collaborator aware of the storage location for their data.

This is especially important if code is being produced. If the need for a version control system is found, also defines a robust (possible) solution for the issue, such as a Version Control System software. May or may not reference every data type/format combination.
criteria.rationale: File versioning can quickly get out of hand if not addressed promptly and with a specific solution.

criteria.description: Specifically indicates which labelling strategy will be used for physical and digital samples. This refers specifically to sample, aliquot or observation identifiers. These identifiers may or may not be persistent or globally unique (see C.org.7), but must be unique in the context of the project. Identifies a solution to assure local uniqueness.
criteria.rationale: Identification of samples is essential for data and metadata cross-referencing. Identifiers must be at least locally unique to be useful, and a centralized method to check this uniqueness is essential, especially if sampling occurs simultaneously.

criteria.title: Uses interoperable identifiers for metadata
criteria.scoring: Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description:
Similar to C.inter.2. The identifiers used for metadata definitions (e.g. column names) are interoperable. For example, they use URLs or semantics which refer to shared, community definitions. Also fulfilled if the problem is taken into consideration and no standard definitions are applicable (See also C.meta.2).
The interoperability of any specific identifier is left to reviewer expertise.
criteria.rationale: Usage of interoperable definitions for data characteristics is essential for FAIR Interoperability.

criteria.title: Indicates if calibration is needed and how it will be done

Moreover, these solutions fulfill minimum usability requirements posed by the handled data (in terms of volume, privacy sensibility, legal requirement, access permission needs, etc...). The judgement on suitability of a certain solution to the data handled by the project is left to reviewer expertise.
criteria.rationale: The choice of hot data storage is essential for proper RDM and underlines all other choices.

criteria.title: Addresses the need of a (meta)data backup policy during the project

This criterium is also fulfilled if no backups are required, although why this is the case should be properly argumented.
criteria.rationale: Data backups are essential to avoid data loss due to damages or accidental deletion or modification, especially for high-value data which is impossible or costly to replace.

criteria.title: Indicates the owner(s) of the data

Indicates explicitly who is legally the owner of the data. This is especially important when human data is handled and, in any case, identifies who must be contacted if issues related to data arise. To be fulfilled, contact information of the owner must be provided.
Note that the researcher(s) who generate the data might not be their owners, as contractual obligations might transfer their ownerships to e.g. their institutions. If data ownership is ambiguous, a data sharing agreement should be created to address it.
criteria.rationale: A specific data owner is required to dispel any possible future disputes, legal or otherwise. It also makes it clear who must be contacted before publishing or sharing the data.

criteria.description: Indicates if a consortium-level formal data sharing agreement will have to be created, and if so, who is responsible to create it. This is most often done to delineate who is the owner of which dataset.
criteria.rationale: Same rationale as E.owner.1, just applied to consortia.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: A data sharing agreement will be created by the Principal Investigator to delineate how data will be shared and owned by the various consortium partners before month 6 of the project.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Data ownership is not taken in consideration.*
*Nobody is given explicit responsibility in creating the agreement.*
*Consortium-level data sharing policies are not delineated.*

criteria.title: Addresses licensing issues (or lack thereof) of reused data
criteria.description: Considers if specific licenses are applies to the reused data, and how they will be followed during the project. This is especially important if Share-alike clauses are included in reused data. Score as fulfilled if one of the selection criteria for reusable data is that only CC-0 data will be used.
criteria.rationale: Some licenses impose new limitations on data handling of new data, especially if they are combined with it.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: This project will consider for reuse only CC0 data.
No data can/will be reused, so there will be no issues regarding existing data licensing.
All data produced using CC-BY-SA data will also be made available openly under the same license.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Reused data licensing is not addressed.*

criteria.title: Addresses ethical concerns (or lack thereof)
criteria.description: Considers if the data may have ethical concerns regarding its acquisition or handling. Ethical concerns may arise due to the nature of the experiment, the nature of the subjects of the experiment or other circumstances.
criteria.rationale: Knowing if ethical concerns might be involved in the running of experiments is a necessary prerequisites of handling them properly.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: As experiments involve macaques, ethical concerns are expected to arise.
As only cell lines will be handled during the project, no ethical concerns are expected.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Ethical concerns are not discussed.*

criteria.title: Addresses the need to contact the ethical board
criteria.scoring: Applicable only if ethical concerns are envisioned (see E.ethics.1). Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: If ethical concerns might arise, considers if the ethical board must be contacted, and if so by whom, how, and with which deadline.
criteria.rationale: Ethical boards must be contacted if ethics concerns have to be addressed.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: The ethics board in the University will be contacted to give an opinion and approval of all experiments involving animals.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Ethical concerns are not discussed.*
*Contacting ethical boards is not discussed.*

criteria.title: Addresses how ethic concerns affect data sharing
criteria.scoring: Applicable only if ethical concerns are envisioned (see E.ethics.1). Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: If ethical concerns might arise, considers how these may affect data sharing and reuse. If possible, details methods to reduce or remove these limitations.
criteria.rationale: Some ethical concerns (e.g. handling of protected species, specific wording of informed consent, de-anonymization concerns) might limit data sharing.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: As we believe that this data might potentially foster marginalization of a minority, we will not share it openly but only upon request.
The political survey data which will be collected will not be shared, even anonymously. This was done to prevent possible repercussions on the population.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Ethical concerns are not discussed.*

criteria.title: Describes which data can be shared and which can't
criteria.scoring: Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: For each data type and format combination, details which data can be openly shared and which cannot be shared, or must be placed under and embargo or other access restrictions.
criteria.rationale: Clearly stating which data will be shared promotes openness and requires follow-up at the end of the project.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: All datasets will be openly shared after the end of the project.
All datasets will be shared openly, with the exception of the measuring apparatus blueprints, which will be placed under embargo for up to 4 years pending patenting.

examples.title: Partially Fulfilled examples
examples: *Only some data types are addressed.*
Sharing of data will be taken in consideration after the end of the project *(Too vague*)*.*

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No consideration on data availability is given.*

criteria.title: IA - Indicates why data cannot be shared openly
criteria.scoring: Only applicable if some (meta)data types cannot be shared. Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: For each data type which will not be shared openly, specifies why this is the case. This does not include the metadata on the specific data type (see F.open.3).
criteria.rationale: A reason to *not* share must be given to follow the “as open as possible, as closed as necessary” philosophy.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: All datasets will be shared openly, with the exception of the measuring apparatus blueprints, which will be placed under embargo for up to 4 years pending patenting.

examples.title: Partially Fulfilled examples
examples: *Only some data types are addressed.*
Sharing of data will be taken in consideration after the end of the project *(Too vague*)*.*

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No consideration on data availability is given.*

criteria.title: IA - Indicates why metadata cannot be shared openly
criteria.scoring: Only applicable if some (meta)data types cannot be shared. Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: For each data type which will not be shared openly, specifies why even metadata cannot be shared. Not fulfilled if even one metadata type which is not shared is not accompanied by an adequate description of the reasons for not sharing.
criteria.rationale: A reason to *not* share must be given to follow the “as open as possible, as closed as necessary” philosophy. Metadata can (and should) usually be shared even if the data is under embargo or cannot be shared for some other reason.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: *Some valid reason not to share metadata, which currently I cannot come up with.*

examples.title: Partially Fulfilled examples
examples: *Only some data types are addressed.*
Sharing of data will be taken in consideration after the end of the project *(Too vague*)*.*

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No consideration on (meta)data availability is given.*

criteria.title: IA - Indicates how data sharing restrictions will be minimized
criteria.scoring: Only applicable if some (meta)data types cannot be shared. Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description:
Explicitly indicates how data sharing limitations will be reduced or overcome. Also fulfilled if potential strategies to overcome these limitations will be tested after data collection.
Reason: Methods like anonymization and summarization can be used to overcome most data sharing limitations. Requiring an explicit mention of possible ways to increase data sharing forces the authors to take it into consideration.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data anonymization will be attempted at the end of the project to allow data sharing. However, at least k=10 will be required for security reasons. If this is not achievable, the data will be kept accessible only under request.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Data sharing limitations are not discussed.*
*Ways to keep sharing data are not taken into consideration or planned.*

criteria.title: Describes the process followed to decide which data to preserve
criteria.description: Specifies how data will be selected for preservation, or, alternatively, if all data should be preserved and why that is the case.
criteria.rationale: Not all data must be preserved for long periods of time. As data preservation is a time-consuming, costly endeavor, selection of which data is worth preserving and for how long should be explicit. Note that replication of the study is almost always required, thus most generated data will need to be preserved, even for a limited period of time.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data regarding the detected economic trends is expected to be potentially useful in the future, even for historic reasons, so it will be preserved in perpetuity. Data regarding local stock exchanges will be preserved for 5 years for reproducibility purposes.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Selection of data for preservation is not discussed.*
All data will be preserved indefinitely *(too vague).*

criteria.title: Considers the target audience of reusers of the preserved data
criteria.description: Discusses who might be interested in reusing the shared data, other than for reproducibility purposes.
criteria.rationale: Discussing this point explicitly forces the author to think why they are sharing the data, and for what (re-usability) purpose.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data regarding the detected economic trends could be reused by economists to generate new trend models, and by historians to describe the current economic growth rates.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Selection of data for preservation is not discussed.*
*Description of potential target audiences for reuse is not given.*

criteria.title: Indicates which data must be destroyed for legal reasons, and why
criteria.scoring: Only applicable if some (meta)data types cannot be shared. Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled), 0.5 (partially fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: Discusses why some (meta)data must be destroyed for legal reasons and why this is the case.
criteria.rationale: Some contractual or other legal obligations (e.g. too many privacy concerns) require data to be destroyed. Keeping this in mind and addressing it specifically can reduce the potential disruptive effect this destruction might have on using the data for the project and beyond.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Patient identification data will be destroyed as soon as pseudonymization is performed, as there is not need for it for the purposes of this project.

examples.title: Partially Fulfilled examples
examples: *Only some data types are addressed.*

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No consideration on (meta)data availability is given.*

criteria.title: Indicates for how long data will be preserved
criteria.description: Defines for how long data will be preserved. For long-term data preservation, at least 13 years must be guaranteed. This is generally applicable to all data as a whole, so partial fulfillment does not apply. If data preservation length is specified for only some preserved data types, score this as not fulfilled.
criteria.rationale: Not all data must be preserved for long periods of time. As data preservation is a time-consuming, costly endeavor, selection of which data is worth preserving and for how long should be explicit. Note that replication of the study is almost always required, thus most generated data will need to be preserved, even for a limited period of time.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data regarding the detected economic trends is expected to be potentially useful in the future, even for historic reasons, so it will be preserved in perpetuity. Data regarding local stock exchanges will be preserved for 5 years for reproducibility purposes.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Selection of data for preservation is not discussed.*
All data will be preserved indefinitely *(too vague).*

criteria.title: Indicates when the data will be made available
criteria.description: Defines when (meta)data will be made available. This can happen as soon as the data is collected, at the end of the project, or after a (finite) predetermined duration. This is generally applicable to all data as a whole, so partial fulfillment does not apply. If data preservation length is specified for only some preserved data types, score this as not fulfilled.
criteria.rationale: Determining in the DMP when the (meta)data will be made available makes the commitment tangible and the authors accountable for it.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data will be made available after publication (at most one year after the project ends).
Metadata regarding the collected data will be made available immediately after validation and quality assurance. Data, on the other hand, will be placed under a 5-year embargo.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Dates of availability are not explicitely discussed.*

criteria.title: If delayed, indicates why the data will be embargoed
criteria.scoring: Only applicable if some data is not immediately made available. Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description: Specifies why (meta)data cannot be made immediately available.
criteria.rationale: Considering this point explicitly should be done in order to follow the “as open as possible, as closed as necessary” philosophy.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Metadata regarding the collected data will be made available immediately after validation and quality assurance. Data, on the other hand, will be placed under a 5-year embargo to allow the creation of scientific publications. After publication, embargo will end.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Dates of availability are not explicitly discussed.*
Metadata regarding the collected data will be made available immediately after validation and quality assurance. Data, on the other hand, will be placed under a 5-year embargo.

criteria.title: If not via direct access, indicates how the data will be made accessible
criteria.scoring: Applicable only is direct download of (meta)data is not possible, but access is still given. Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description:
Specifies which method(s) should be used to access data which is not available for direct download. If possible, also mentions the requirements needed by those asking for access to obtain it. If money is required for data transfer, also indicates why this is the case.
This information can be omitted only if a completely automatic way to obtain (controlled) access is available, in which absolutely no human interaction is required).
This is generally applicable to all data as a whole, so partial fulfillment does not apply. If access methods are specified for only some preserved data types, score this as not fulfilled.
criteria.rationale: Accessibility is not necessarily only when data is directly obtainable. However, when this is not the case (need for data transfer agreements, sensitive data, large datasets), the specific way in which data can be obtained should be extremely clear.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data regarding migratory routes will be kept confidential for security concerns. It will be provided upon reasonable request for academic purposes. Details of reuse purposes must be given, and a data transfer agreement will be signed.
Data is too large to be uploaded to a repository for direct access. Access will be given by shipping copies of it in hard-drives or other physical support upon request.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Accessibility methods are not discussed.*
Data access will be given upon reasonable request *(not enough information).*

criteria.title: If not shared openly, indicates who is responsible to keep the data Accessible for the long term.
criteria.scoring: Applicable only is direct download of (meta)data is not possible, but access is still given. Scored as either 0 (not fulfilled) or 1 (fulfilled).
criteria.description:
Access methods for non-direct download data includes the names and contact information of those responsible to give access to the data in the long-term, or, alternatively, of the offices designated to carry it out.
This information can be omitted only if a completely automatic way to obtain (controlled) access is available, in which absolutely no human interaction is required).

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Data regarding migratory routes will be kept confidential for security concerns. It will be provided upon reasonable request for academic purposes by contacting J.M Rodriguez (jm.rodriguez@institution.org) or the institutions RDM office (rdm@institution.org). Details of reuse purposes must be given, and a data transfer agreement will be signed.

Data is too large to be uploaded to a repository for direct access. Access will be given by shipping copies of it in hard-drives or other physical support upon request. Contact J.M Rodriguez (jm.rodriguez@institution.org) or the institutions RDM office (rdm@institution.org) for information and shipping and handling costs.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Accessibility methods are not discussed.*
Data access will be given upon reasonable request *(not enough information).*

Data regarding migratory routes will be kept confidential for security concerns. It will be provided upon reasonable request for academic purposes. Details of reuse purposes must be given, and a data transfer agreement will be signed *(No contact information*)*.*

criteria.title: Indicates how the data will be findable by interested parties
criteria.description:
Indicates how the (meta)data will be findable by others. This includes sharing the data in a searchable repository, using specific metadata, advertising the data on social media, data-specific publications in data journals, conference proceedings, etc...
Sufficiency of this effort is left to reviewer expertise.
criteria.rationale: Provisions to make potentially interested reusers aware of the availability of the data should be arranged to increase the value of the data and the probability of reuse.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: To increase findability, (meta)data will be indexed in ArchiRepo, the open repository of architectural information.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Dates of availability are not explicitly discussed.*
Metadata regarding the collected data will be made available immediately after validation and quality assurance. Data, on the other hand, will be placed under a 5-year embargo.

criteria.title: Indicates how PIDs will be used, and which PID service will be used
criteria.description: Indicates which Persistent Identifiers (PIDs) will be used, how, and which PID-minting service will be employed to generate them. If applicable, should also consider the cost of using such a PID service.
criteria.rationale: Persistent Identifiers (PIDs) are a must when dealing with data, as the unambiguously refer to one and only one concept. Their thoughtful use is essential to both manage local data effectively and share it afterwards.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: The project will use locally minted PIDs for sample labelling, their minting provided manually via a master document.
The project will use DOIs for final deliverable, minted by doi.org.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Usage of PIDs is not envisioned.*
Permanent Identifiers will be used when possible (*Too generic*).

criteria.title: Indicates how data and metadata will be linked
criteria.description: Specifies the way in which metadata will be linked to the data and, if possible, a way to link the metadata to the data.
criteria.rationale: FAIR principle F.3 *“Metadata clearly and explicitly include the identifier of the data they describe”* requires this step, but, in general, links from the metadata to the data should be present at the very minimum to increase data findability. Additionally, it makes it very difficult to mistake which metadata refers to which data, and vice-versa.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Metadata will contain the resolvable PIDs of the data they refer to. Tabular data cannot contain backlinks, but they will be provided as deposition metadata.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No discussion of data-to-metadata linking.*

criteria.title: Indicates how metadata will be indexed and made searchable
criteria.description: Indicates an (online) service which indexes and allows searching through the metadata. This service should be available for the foreseeable future and provide a robust, complete search feature (i.e. other than title-based). Also details how the metadata will be supported by the platform hosting it, and to which degree it will be interoperable with other similar datasets.
criteria.rationale: Metadata should be indexed and searchable, even if the data is not.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: Our metadata is mostly compatible with the BWX repository and will be indexed properly. However, as some fields are not supported, the whole metadata files will be reuploaded in their entirety to allow more complete indexing.
Zenodo allows a number of custom fields, however, the metadata interoperability of the platform is limited. We will collect all metadata into a single file to allow easier (local) searching.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *Metadata is not collected.*
*Discussion on the integration of the platform with the metadata is not done.*

criteria.title: Identifies an accredited repository for data preservation
criteria.description:
Identifies a satisfactory, accredited repository to preserve data. Arguments why this choice was made and outlines the related costs.
Criteria for “satisfactory” and “accredited” are left to reviewer expertise, but consider relevance to the topic, scientific field, prestige and trustworthiness of the institution behind the repository, and more.
criteria.rationale: A good data repository can make or break preservation efforts. It is important the sufficient thought and care is given when selecting one.

examples.title: Fulfilled examples
examples: As no relevant topical repository was found, we will use Zenodo as a data preservation service. As the volume of data is small, no costs are projected.

All sequencing data will be stored in the European Nucleotide Archive. All metadata required by the portal will be uploaded directly as such, and extra metadata fields will be deposited in Zenodo, containing backlinks to the ENA depositions.

examples.title: Not fulfilled examples
examples: *No discussion of repositories is done.*

criteria.title: Addresses who is responsible for capturing data
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for acquiring and saving data.

criteria.title: Addresses who is responsible for assessing data quality
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for developing data quality guidelines (if not already done in the DMP), develop data quality assessment software and, in general, be responsible for data quality.

criteria.title: Addresses who is responsible for sharing data
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for sharing the data following the provisions of the DMP. These individuals are also those that can be contacted if the data was not shared in a timely or satisfying manner.

criteria.title: Addresses who is responsible for data safety and security
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for ensuring data safety and security.

criteria.title: Addresses who is responsible for data backup and integrity
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for performing data backups and ensuring integrity. If these services are offloaded to someone external, names the specific companies or institutions.

criteria.title: Indicates who is overviewing the implementation of the DMP
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for implementing the strategies defined in the DMP. Most often, this is the individual responsible for the project, the Principal Investigator.

criteria.title: Indicates who is responsible for reviewing and revising the DMP
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for updating the DMP, if it is needed. Most often this coincides with G.resp.6.

criteria.title: Indicates who will pledge time to data curation
criteria.description: Names the individual(s) which will perform and be responsible for curating data, including preprocessing, obfuscation, and other data-related functions outside of analysis.
criteria.rationale: Data curation takes time and effort, especially if format modifications or controlled preprocessing has to be performed during the project or to enable data sharing.

criteria.title: Indicates which costs are related to data storage
criteria.description: Indicates the (projected) costs of hot data storage (i.e. storage during the project).

criteria.title: Indicates which costs are related to data preservation and sharing
criteria.description: Indicates the (projected) costs of cold data storage (i.e. storage after the project).

criteria.title: Indicates which costs are related to hiring data professionals
criteria.description: Indicates if hiring data curation professionals (i.e. data stewards) is required, and if so for how long and with which economic expenditure.
